document.title: Comments of the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio's Office of the Federal Energy Advocate in response to FERC's 02/20/2025 Order

)

)

Facilities

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

COMMENTS OF THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF OHIO’S  
OFFICE OF THE FEDERAL ENERGY ADVOCATE 
 
The Office of the Federal Energy Advocate (Ohio FEA) of the Public Utilities 
Commission of Ohio, fulfilling its statutory duty to advocate on behalf of Ohio’s retail electricity 
consumers,1 submits the following in response to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(FERC or Commission) February 20, 2025 Order instituting a show cause proceeding pursuant to 
section 206 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) regarding large loads co-located at generating 
facilities in the PJM Interconnection, LLC (PJM) region. 
I. 
Background 
The substantial grid challenges PJM is working to address are well known and a result of 
numerous simultaneous issues, including a changing generation resource mix, delayed capacity 
auctions, lengthy interconnection queue reform, and unprecedented forecasted load growth 
driven primarily by data centers. Given the current landscape of tight supply and increasing 
demand, interest in the topic of co-locating large loads with generating facilities in PJM has 
 
1 Ohio Revised Code 4928.24.

2 
escalated over the last two years. On November 1, 2024, the Commission convened a technical 
conference in Docket No. AD24-11-000 related to large loads co-located at generating facilities, 
followed by a request for post-technical conference comments.2 Separately, on November 22, 
2024, Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (Constellation) filed an FPA section 206 complaint 
against PJM in Docket No. EL25-20-000 arguing that PJM’s Tariff is unjust, unreasonable, and 
unduly discriminatory because it does not contain rules for interconnected generators to follow 
when they seek to execute certain configurations and arrangements to serve co-located load.3  
In the instant proceedings, the Commission consolidated the show cause proceeding with 
the technical conference and Constellation complaint proceeding for administrative efficiency 
and directed PJM and the Transmission Owners to respond to enumerated questions and 
concerns regarding co-location arrangements.  
The Ohio FEA offers the following comments for FERC’s consideration. 
II. 
Comments 
A. 
Multiple Pathways Are Needed to Address Resource Adequacy Needs. 
The PJM region faces the unprecedented challenge of simultaneously managing 
significant load growth, premature retirement of dispatchable thermal generation, and slow entry 
of new resource additions. Significant incremental capacity is needed, and the Ohio FEA 
appreciates PJM’s effort in working with stakeholders, state regulators, and the Commission to 
effectuate market, planning, and operations reforms to ensure that resource adequacy and grid 
reliability are maintained. 
 
2 Docket No. AD24-11-000.  
3 Docket No. EL25-20-000.

3 
Given PJM’s existing market conditions and speed to market concerns, it is not surprising 
that various permutations of co-locating load with generation resources have recently come to 
the forefront. The Ohio FEA agrees that an “all hands on deck” approach is needed to meet 
supply and demand challenges in the region and appreciates PJM’s commitment “to facilitating 
and supporting co-location arrangements where permitted by applicable state law.”4 However, 
PJM must develop transparent processes to assess the grid impacts of co-location arrangements 
and to ensure that individual arrangements do not threaten grid reliability or worsen the resource 
adequacy concerns that exist across the region.  
In its answer, PJM lays out eight potential options for large load co-location 
configurations, including the existing standard process for integrating large loads into the grid 
(regardless of whether co-located generation shares the same point of interconnection) and the 
traditional behind-the-meter configuration where generation that serves a primary customer is 
netted against that customer’s use of the electric grid. PJM goes on to describe five conceptual 
options that are not in its current Tariff but that might be of interest to states or entities 
contemplating alternative co-location arrangements and seeking clarity from PJM or the 
Commission.  
Through its discussion of the range of options, PJM reiterates its recommendation and 
preference that large loads be designated as Network Load as opposed to configurations that 
propose to install off-system load behind an existing generator.5 “Network Load status offers the 
most robust reliability benefits and holistic planning efficiencies, minimizes the need for one-off 
 
4 PJM Answer at 32.  
5 A configuration where both the load and the generator are isolated from the grid is not addressed in PJM’s Answer.

4 
operational procedures (both interim and longer term), and offers a cost allocation framework 
that assesses charges for use of and reliance on the transmission system.”6  
The Ohio FEA shares concern that installing large off-system loads behind existing 
generators adds complexity, including that the load would not be captured in the annual load 
forecasting and planning processes conducted by Load Serving Entities and PJM. Additionally, 
the Ohio FEA notes an important difference between new loads that are paired with new 
generation and co-location arrangements that propose to take existing generation off the system. 
The latter has broader implications because it would change the power flow across the 
transmission system and affect the mix of resources available to participate in PJM’s energy and 
capacity markets. Because of the wider range of impact, co-location arrangements that take 
existing generation off the system should be subject to robust analysis before they are allowed to 
proceed, including studying the impacts on the markets, grid reliability, and resource adequacy. 
B. 
Bring Your Own Generation (BYOG) Should Be Encouraged.  
In encouraging load additions to be Network Load, PJM acknowledges that any 
additional load on the system requires either the addition of supply resources to serve that load or 
flexibility on the part of the load to curtail its consumption from the transmission system when 
necessary to maintain reliability.7 Three of the five conceptual options PJM outlines in its 
Answer could serve to bring new Network Load on faster without exacerbating resource 
adequacy concerns. The Ohio FEA supports further consideration of these options.  
In particular, co-located load that elects to be Network Load and brings its own 
generation, or BYOG, could augment the steps PJM is already taking, such as through the 
 
6 PJM Answer at Exhibit B at 2. 
7 PJM Answer at 62.

5 
Reliability Resource Initiative, to ensure that needed generation resources can be timely 
integrated onto the transmission system to serve significant future load growth. BYOG may 
provide a pathway in some states for new generation resources to support co-located load and 
also serve as PJM Capacity Resources. Under this option, various incentives could be explored, 
including faster processing of generation that enters the PJM interconnection queue to 
accommodate the co-located load. Importantly, under BYOG, the new Network Load would 
bring generation resources that could also serve as Capacity Resources, mitigating both local grid 
impacts at the point of interconnection and regional resource adequacy concerns.  
C. 
Co-Located Load Must Pay for Grid Services Used. 
The Ohio FEA agrees with PJM that “participants involved in co-location arrangements 
should pay the costs of any grid services they consume and the arrangements must be reliable 
and operationally manageable.”8 Regardless of the co-located load configurations that may be 
approvable by the Commission and under state laws, PJM must establish transparent processes to 
determine the extent to which individual co-located load relies on the bulk power system (for 
Ancillary Services or otherwise) and a means by which to allocate those transmission costs 
accordingly so that co-located load arrangements do not shift costs to other customers.  
III. 
Conclusion 
The Ohio FEA appreciates the Commission’s thorough investigation into issues 
surrounding co-located loads to assist PJM and state regulators in meeting the resource adequacy 
needs of the region without compromising reliability.

6
